documents.title: AI Teaching and Research Guidance
documents.summary: The Center for Faculty Excellence page states that OU does not mandate one approach to AI in teaching. It asks faculty to make discipline-appropriate choices and tell students, and it lists workshops, consultations, a Canvas course and AI literacy frameworks.
documents.stance_why: The page says "OU does not mandate a single approach to AI in the classroom" and that faculty "are encouraged to make intentional, discipline-appropriate choices," so it sets no stance itself and hands the decision to instructors: delegates.

units.why: The sentence says "OU does not mandate a single approach to AI in the classroom," so the university sets no campus-wide rule and leaves the choice to instructors; that is the instructor-decides type (P04), stated as a fact.
units.anchor: OU does not mandate a single approach to AI in the classroom.

units.why: The opening sentence frames AI as raising "important questions about learning goals, assessment, authorship, and academic integrity" but sets no rule; no type captures a bare framing of issues, so it is UNCOVERED rather than stretched.
units.anchor: AI raises important questions about learning goals, assessment, authorship, and academic integrity.
units.uncovered_note: Names the issues AI raises (learning goals, assessment, authorship, integrity) as context for instructor choices, without a rule.

units.why: Faculty "are encouraged to make intentional, discipline-appropriate choices," a recommendation that each instructor decide for their discipline, so P04 (instructor sets the rule) with modality should.
units.anchor: faculty are encouraged to make intentional, discipline-appropriate choices

units.why: Faculty are encouraged "to communicate those choices clearly to students," a duty to make expectations explicit. P09 is the nearest type but it asks for a syllabus statement specifically, whereas this is general communication.
units.anchor: to communicate those choices clearly to students.
units.fit_note: Asks instructors to communicate their choices clearly to students but does not name the syllabus.

units.why: The CFE offers a Canvas course for faculty that "addresses key topics related to Generative AI and teaching in higher education"; this is faculty learning support (P63), provided by an office (admin).
units.anchor: addresses key topics related to Generative AI and teaching in higher education.
units.policy: The CFE provides a Canvas course, Generative AI at the University, that addresses key topics related to Generative AI and teaching in higher education.

units.why: The Canvas course "also has example Generative AI Policy language for your syllabus," so the institution supplies sample syllabus language, exactly P110.
units.anchor: example Generative AI Policy language for your syllabus

units.why: "Faculty members can also schedule consultations on AI in" teaching is an offer of one-to-one help for instructors, which is faculty support (P63).
units.anchor: Faculty members can also schedule consultations on AI in

units.why: "Watch for CFE workshops and learning communities on AI-related topics" points faculty to workshops and learning communities, named in the P63 definition.
units.anchor: Watch for CFE workshops
units.policy: Faculty are told to watch for CFE workshops and learning communities on AI-related topics.

units.why: Faculty are "encouraged to consider how AI affects assignment design, assessment strategies, and the kinds of learning they most want students to demonstrate"; this asks instructors to rethink assessment around AI (P35), but only to consider it, not to redesign.
units.anchor: encouraged to consider how AI affects assignment design, assessment strategies
units.fit_note: Encourages considering the effect of AI on assignments and assessment; it does not prescribe a redesign.

units.why: The page lists AI literacy frameworks that "can inform course outcomes, assignment design, departmental conversations, or grant narratives," which directs readers to further resources (P115).
units.anchor: These frameworks can inform course outcomes, assignment design, departmental conversations

units.why: Faculty "are encouraged to consult OU guidance and campus experts before integrating AI into research workflows or grant proposals," a rule about AI in research and grants (P62).
units.anchor: encouraged to consult OU guidance and campus experts before integrating AI into research workflows

units.why: The CFE has "a faculty fellow specifically for AI-related subjects" and says consultations "do not require a commitment to using AI," which is faculty support for learning about AI (P63).
units.anchor: Consultations are exploratory in nature and do not require a commitment to using AI

documents.title: Generative AI Policy examples (July 2025)
documents.summary: The CFE supplies six sample syllabus policies for instructors, from a full ban to full use and required exploration, based on the AI Assessment Scale. Each pairs rules and consequences with a statement of the instructor's own AI use.
documents.stance_why: The document offers six sample statements ("five policy examples based on the AI Assessment Scale ... and a sixth" that varies by assignment) for instructors to choose from, so it takes no stance of its own and lists tiers: delegates.

units.why: The heading says the Generative AI Policy is a "required component" whose text may vary if it is "explicit," so instructors must state an AI policy in the syllabus (P09).
units.anchor: required component, text may vary and could be included, as long as it is explicit

units.why: Instructors "are encouraged to have Generative AI policies for each assignment," going beyond the syllabus; P09 (state expectations in syllabus or assignment instructions) fits.
units.anchor: you are encouraged to have Generative AI policies for each assignment in your class

units.why: The text says explaining "how Generative AI could, but shouldn’t, be used, and why" helps students "even if you choose to implement a Generative AI ban"; this is explaining the rules to students (P66).
units.anchor: explaining how Generative AI could, but shouldn’t, be used, and why

units.why: It notes AI "is increasingly integrated into search tools, e-books, Microsoft and Google products," signalling that rules must cover embedded AI (P07), but states no rule here.
units.anchor: Generative AI is increasingly integrated into search tools, e-books, Microsoft and Google products
units.fit_note: Only notes that AI is embedded in common tools; it states no rule about them here.

units.why: The CFE "provided five policy examples" for instructors to adopt, i.e. sample syllabus language and templates (P110).
units.anchor: We’ve provided five policy examples based on the AI Assessment Scale

units.why: The AI Assessment Scale supplies named levels of AI use for policy on assessments and "may also be used across your course," a tiered framework (P05).
units.anchor: The AI Assessment Scale was intended to be used for policy guidance on individual assessments

units.why: "You may also want to mix and match the sample statements" leaves the choice and blend of rules to each instructor (P04).
units.anchor: You may also want to mix and match the sample statements

units.why: The restricted sample justifies a ban with "We learn best when we are actively engaged in the process," i.e. doing the work yourself builds skill (P41).
units.anchor: We learn best when we are actively engaged in the process of completing all aspects

units.why: The sample states that using Generative AI, "including, but not limited to, ChatGPT, CoPilot, ClaudeAI, Gemini, and Grammarly AI, is considered a violation of the academic integrity policy for this course"; a default ban (P01) that also classes use as misconduct, but the ban is the rule being set.
units.anchor: is considered a violation of the academic integrity policy for this course

units.why: The ban "includes using Generative AI to write outlines, conduct research, to write or edit your papers": AI may not produce or edit submitted work, so P19, with outlines, research and editing also named.
units.anchor: this includes using Generative AI to write outlines, conduct research, to write or edit your
units.fit_note: Also bans AI for outlines, research and editing, wider than producing submitted work.

units.why: The ban also covers using AI "to take your quizzes or exams," which is the no-AI-on-assessments type (P22).
units.anchor: to take your quizzes or exams

units.why: Under the ban, students with an AI-integrated e-book or search engine "should not rely on the Generative AI output"; this covers AI embedded in tools (P07).
units.anchor: you should not rely on the Generative AI output and engage instead with the source
units.fit_note: Allows the tool but tells students to engage with source material rather than rely on the AI output.

units.why: "Assignments have been designed to either occur in a controlled environment (such as in-class or with Lockdown Browser)" shows assessment moved to controlled, unassisted settings (P33).
units.anchor: assignments have been designed to either occur in a controlled environment
units.fit_note: Also says assignments are designed so AI is unlikely to succeed.

units.why: The sample lists the "Academic Success Center, the Writing Center" and other human supports "where you might otherwise want to use Generative AI," pointing students to human help (P72).
units.anchor: Resources are available to help you where you might otherwise want to use Generative AI

units.why: "If you have any questions about this policy or what counts as Generative AI, please talk with me" tells students to ask the instructor, so P10.
units.anchor: If you have any questions about this policy or what counts as Generative AI, please

units.why: "Could result in a zero for an assignment or a failing grade on the course" states concrete penalties in advance (P37).
units.anchor: could result in a zero for an assignment or a failing grade on the course

units.why: "Any usage of Generative AI in this course may be considered a violation of the academic integrity policy" classifies use under the ban as misconduct (P36).
units.anchor: Any usage of Generative AI in this course may be considered a violation of the

units.why: "I will not use Generative AI to aid in my teaching, grading, or in my communication with you" is the instructor committing to limits on their own AI use, tied to the ban (P47).
units.anchor: I will not use Generative AI to aid in my teaching, grading, or in my
units.fit_note: Also commits the instructor not to use AI for grading, which overlaps P46.

units.why: The planning sample says AI "can be very useful as you plan your strategy" for an assignment and lists allowed uses, a permissive default limited to planning (P02).
units.anchor: Generative AI can be very useful as you plan your strategy for how to approach
units.fit_note: Permits AI for planning and gathering information only, not a general default.

units.why: The sample points students to Goblin.tools "Magic ToDo" to "break down more complicated tasks into smaller action items"; AI for planning an approach, nearest P15.
units.anchor: Goblin.tools has a “Magic ToDo”, which can help you break down more complicated tasks
units.fit_note: AI for breaking a task into steps, not brainstorming ideas.

units.why: "You may use Generative AI to help you in the initial stages of your assignments" allows brainstorming and outlining, which is P15.
units.anchor: You may use Generative AI to help you in the initial stages of your assignments

units.why: Brainstorming means "thinking with Generative AI, rather than having Generative AI think for you"; students stay the primary thinker (P32).
units.anchor: brainstorming means thinking with Generative AI, rather than having Generative AI think for you

units.why: The sample advises "you should provide more context in your prompt, share your interests, your ideas," which is advice on how to prompt (P93).
units.anchor: you should provide more context in your prompt, share your interests, your ideas, what questions

units.why: "We will explore ResearchRabbit, SemanticScholar, AI research assistants in e-books" to "find additional sources" is AI for literature search (P104).
units.anchor: AI Research tools: We will explore ResearchRabbit, SemanticScholar, AI research assistants in e-books

units.why: "You may only use free Generative AI tools, or those that are provided to you through the university" is justified by "To ensure everyone has access to the same resources," an equity rule (P51); P92 also fits, but the stated reason is equal access.
units.anchor: To ensure everyone has access to the same resources, you may only use free Generative
units.fit_note: Restricts students to free or university-provided tools so access is equal.

units.why: "We will have ongoing discussions in class about effective use of Generative AI" commits the instructor to discussing AI with students (P66).
units.anchor: we will have ongoing discussions in class about effective use of Generative AI

units.why: Students "will be asked to reflect frequently about AI usage" and "share your prompts, screenshots of your chats," which requires logs and reflections (P26).
units.anchor: share your prompts, screenshots of your chats with Generative AI tools

units.why: "You should not use AI to draft or revise your writing" bars AI from producing or editing the student’s own prose, so P19 with modality should-not.
units.anchor: you should not use AI to draft or revise your writing
units.fit_note: Specifically drafting and revising writing.

units.why: "There may be times, such as in-class quizzes, midterms, or finals, where Generative AI usage is prohibited" bans AI on assessments (P22).
units.anchor: in-class quizzes, midterms, or finals, where Generative AI usage is prohibited

units.why: "You will be responsible for the accuracy of anything you submit" makes students own what they submit (P29).
units.anchor: you will be responsible for the accuracy of anything you submit
units.fit_note: Responsibility is for accuracy, including citing and summarizing articles found through AI tools.

units.why: "Must read the material you are citing" requires students to read AI-found sources, which is verifying AI output (P31).
units.anchor: must read the material you are citing

units.why: "Submitting data or research that is not real ... may result in an academic integrity violation for falsifying information" bans fabricated data and names its consequence (P74).
units.anchor: Submitting data or research that is not real (a risk when overly relying on Generative
units.fit_note: Frames fabricated data from AI over-reliance as an integrity violation.

units.why: "I will model appropriate Generative AI usage by clearly disclosing when I use it and why" commits the instructor to disclosing their AI use (P47).
units.anchor: clearly disclosing when I use it and why

units.why: The instructor "will model appropriate Generative AI usage," teaching responsible use by example (P112).
units.anchor: I will model appropriate Generative AI usage

units.why: Expected instructor uses are "to improve the structure of my lectures" and "to find current articles to update our course readings," instructor AI use for teaching work (P59).
units.anchor: using my notes and previous PowerPoints to improve the structure of my lectures

units.why: "I will never use Generative AI to grade your work or to communicate with you" is a commitment that humans grade (P46).
units.anchor: I will never use Generative AI to grade your work or to communicate with you.
units.fit_note: Also covers communication with students.

units.why: The collaboration sample says AI "can be very useful in completing tasks," a permissive default for help with assignments (P02).
units.anchor: Generative AI can be very useful in completing tasks

units.why: Students must "develop and apply the skills you’ll need to appropriately assess and revise any Generative AI outputs," i.e. critically evaluate AI output (P31).
units.anchor: develop and apply the skills you’ll need to appropriately assess and revise any Generative AI

units.why: "You may use Generative AI to help you revise your writing or work on a second draft" allows AI revising support (P91).

units.why: "You are expected to write the first draft yourself" sets a do-it-yourself-first sequence (P90).
units.anchor: you are expected to write the first draft yourself

units.why: Students "maintain the various iterations of your written work so that you can reflect on the changes," keeping drafts and reflections (P26).
units.anchor: maintain the various iterations of your written work so that you can reflect on the

units.why: "You may ask Generative AI to provide you with feedback on your writing or other homework" allows AI feedback on one’s own work; nearest P91 (writing support).
units.anchor: You may ask Generative AI to provide you with feedback on your writing or other
units.fit_note: Feedback on writing and other homework when stuck, not editing.

units.why: "Generative AI is known for sycophancy" and "cannot be relied upon for accuracy," warning that output may mislead (P31).
units.anchor: Generative AI is known for sycophancy
units.fit_note: Warns of sycophancy and loss of individuality rather than telling students to verify.

units.why: "You can work with Generative AI to create study guides based on your own notes" allows study aids (P14).
units.anchor: You can work with Generative AI to create study guides based on your own notes

units.why: "You are encouraged to visit the Writing Center, work with your peers, and review the feedback I provide" points to human help alongside AI (P72).
units.anchor: you are encouraged to visit the Writing Center, work with your peers

units.why: "Deviating from the use cases described here without express permission may be considered a violation" restricts students to listed uses and classes other uses as misconduct (P36).

units.why: Expected instructor uses include "revising quiz or exam questions and responses (with my oversight), drafting case studies or educational games"; instructor AI use for teaching work (P59).
units.anchor: revising quiz or exam questions and responses (with my oversight), drafting case studies or educational
units.fit_note: Includes instructor oversight.

units.why: "May use any free Generative AI tools, including those provided ... by the university" is a permissive default for open use (P02).
units.anchor: May use any free Generative AI tools

units.why: "This will allow everyone in the course to have the same access to Generative AI" gives equal access as the reason for the free-tools limit (P51).
units.anchor: This will allow everyone in the course to have the same access to Generative AI.

units.why: Students "are expected to cite your usage of Generative AI, including any direct quotes or paraphrasing" under class citation guidelines (P24).
units.anchor: Are expected to cite your usage of Generative AI

units.why: Students "must provide a statement at the end of the assignment about your Generative AI usage" written without AI; a disclosure with each submission (P24).
units.anchor: Must provide a statement at the end of the assignment about your Generative AI usage.
units.fit_note: The statement must also be written without AI, as the student’s own reflection.

units.why: The statement "must include: the platform(s) and prompt(s) you used," requiring the tool and prompts to be cited (P25).
units.anchor: the platform(s) and prompt(s) you used

units.why: The statement must include "what additional work you did to verify the output, and to make the work your own," tied to verifying AI output (P31).

units.why: Students reflect on how AI helped them "independently (without the use of Generative AI) achieve the learning objectives of this course," tying AI use to learning objectives (P83).
units.anchor: independently (without the use of Generative AI) achieve the learning objectives of this course

units.why: Students "may also be asked to share your prompts, screenshots of your chats," a possible transcript requirement (P26).
units.anchor: where you may also be asked to share your prompts, screenshots of your chats with

units.why: Expected instructor uses include "graphic design, revising assignment instructions and rubrics" and "receiving feedback on how I communicate with students," instructor AI use for teaching work (P59).
units.anchor: graphic design, revising assignment instructions and rubrics to improve clarity for students

units.why: "I will never use Generative AI to grade your work" (with no bar on communication in this version) is humans assigning grades (P46).

units.anchor: build something novel with Generative AI to satisfy a class assignment

units.why: Students "will reflect frequently about your Generative AI usage, including your process, how you assess accuracy" and document it per assignment, a reflection requirement (P26).
units.anchor: You’ll be asked to reflect frequently about your Generative AI usage, including your process

units.why: "Deviating from the documentation and reflection guidelines provided in each assignment may be considered a violation" makes nondocumentation the violation (P28).
units.anchor: Deviating from the documentation and reflection guidelines provided in each assignment

units.why: Expected instructor uses include "creating Generative AI course tutors," a course-specific AI tool built by the instructor (P17).
units.anchor: creating Generative AI course tutors
units.fit_note: Instructor builds course tutors as part of own AI use; not stated as a tool students must use.

units.why: "Each assignment will have a clear Generative AI policy explaining how it may be used, or not" sets the rule per assignment (P04).

units.anchor: intentionally made to support you in developing the skills and content knowledge

units.why: "Follow assignment instructions carefully, as they will guide you" makes students learn the rules assignment by assignment (P78).

notes: Only the two included documents were coded. The students AI usage guidelines page (KB 3406) was inaccessible behind login. Sample policies are templates for instructors, so unit stances reflect each sample, not a campus-wide rule. Repeated boilerplate sentences across samples (e.g. questions: talk to me) were coded once.
